explanation: You forgot a semicolon (;) at the end of a line. In C, every statement needs to end with ;.
suggestion: Check the line before the error and add a ; at the end.

explanation: The computer does not know what this name means. You used a variable but you never created it with a line like 'int x;'.
suggestion: Check spelling and make sure you write 'int x;' or 'char ch;' to create the variable before you use it.

explanation: You called a function that the computer has not seen before. This often means you forgot to include the header file (like #include <stdio.h>).
suggestion: Add the needed #include at the top, for example #include <stdio.h> for printf or scanf.

patterns: control reaches end of non-void function
non-void function does not return a value
control may reach end of non-void function
explanation: Your function should return a value (like int), but it ends without a 'return' line.
suggestion: Add 'return 0;' or another return value at the end of the function.

explanation: Your program tried to use memory it is not allowed to touch. This crash is called a segmentation fault.
suggestion: Check for mistakes like using a pointer before giving it a value, or going past the end of an array.

explanation: You tried to call a function that the computer does not know. Maybe you misspelled its name or forgot to create it.
suggestion: Check the spelling of the function name. If you made the function yourself, make sure it is written above where you call it, or add a declaration before main().

explanation: You called a function but gave it fewer values (arguments) than it needs.
suggestion: Count how many inputs the function needs and give it all of them, like foo(a, b) instead of foo(a).

explanation: You called a function and gave it more values (arguments) than it expects.
suggestion: Remove the extra value from the function call so the count matches the function's definition.

explanation: You mixed up pointer types. A pointer (address) to one kind of data was used where a different kind was expected.
suggestion: Check the type of the pointer. For example, don't pass 'int *' where 'char *' is needed. Make the types match or use the correct & and * symbols.

explanation: Your printf or scanf format (like %d, %s, %f) does not match the variable type you gave it.
suggestion: Match the % code to the variable: use %d for int, %f for float/double, %s for string (char *), and %c for char.

explanation: You used printf or scanf but the computer cannot find them. You forgot to include their helper file.
suggestion: Add '#include <stdio.h>' at the very top of your file, before main().

explanation: The main() function is written in a wrong way. In C, main should usually be 'int main()' or 'int main(int argc, char *argv[])'.
suggestion: Change your main line to 'int main()' or 'int main(void)' and make sure you have 'return 0;' at the end.

explanation: You tried to access an array position that does not exist. For example, an array of size 5 only has spots 0 to 4.
suggestion: Check your loop and index values. Make sure you never use arr[5] or larger when the size is 5.

explanation: You used a variable before giving it a starting value. It may hold garbage (random) data.
suggestion: Give the variable a value when you create it, like 'int x = 0;' before you use x.

explanation: You created a variable but never used it. It does not break your program, but it is extra code you don't need.
suggestion: Remove the unused variable or use it in your code if you meant to.

explanation: You tried to change a const variable. Const means read-only (locked) and cannot be changed after creation.
suggestion: Do not assign a new value to a const variable. Remove the 'const' word if you need to change it, or use a different variable.

patterns: break statement not within loop or switch
continue statement not within a loop
explanation: You used 'break' or 'continue' outside a loop (for, while) or switch. It only works inside them.
suggestion: Move the break/continue inside the loop body with braces { }, or remove it if you don't need it.

explanation: In a switch case, you missed a 'break;'. The program will slide (fall through) to the next case by mistake.
suggestion: Add 'break;' at the end of each case, or add a comment '// fall through' if you meant it to continue.

explanation: Your function keeps calling itself forever (never stops). This fills up memory and crashes the program.
suggestion: Check your recursive function and make sure it has a clear stopping condition, like 'if (n == 0) return 1;'.

explanation: You tried to divide a number by zero. In math and in C, dividing by zero is not allowed and crashes the program.
suggestion: Before dividing, check if the divisor is zero with 'if (y != 0)' and only divide when it is not zero.

explanation: You used a pointer that points to nothing (NULL). Trying to read or write through it causes a crash.
suggestion: Check if the pointer is NULL before using it: 'if (p != NULL)' and make sure you gave it a real address with malloc or '&'.

explanation: You tried to free (release) the same memory twice, or you used memory after you already freed it.
suggestion: Only call free() once for each malloc(). After free(p), do not use p again and set it to 'p = NULL;'.

explanation: Your number is too big to fit in its type (like int). It wraps around and gives a wrong value.
suggestion: Use a bigger type like 'long long' instead of 'int', or check that the number stays within limits.

explanation: You forgot a closing brace } or bracket ]. Every opening { or [ needs a matching closing one.
suggestion: Count your { and } braces. Add a } at the end of the block where it is missing. Your editor can help highlight matching braces.

explanation: You have an extra semicolon (;) or an extra symbol where it is not needed.
suggestion: Remove the extra ;. For example, don't write 'if (x > 0);' with a ; right after the if condition.
